title: Writing an email
why: Writing to a client or a colleague in French means knowing a set of fixed formulas, from Madame, Monsieur to Cordialement. This lesson gives you the greetings, the polite requests in the conditional, the follow-ups and the closings, so that your emails sound natural from the first line.

{"lessons": ["

Opening a professional email

A French professional email follows set formulas, more than in English. Use them and you will sound competent; forget them and even perfect grammar sounds odd. In France, people say un mail or un e-mail; un courriel is the official word, very common in Quebec.

The greeting

situationFrenchnote
you don't know the nameMadame, Monsieur,the safe choice for a first contact
you know the nameBonjour Madame Martin,the most common today
more formalMadame, / Monsieur,title alone, no name
warmer, after a few exchangesChère Madame, / Cher Monsieur,no surname after cher / chère
a colleagueBonjour Julien,first name, often with tu

Avoid copying English “Dear Ms. Martin”: Chère Madame Martin sounds clumsy to many French readers. Abbreviations are M. (Monsieur, not “Mr”) and Mme (Madame).

The first sentence

Say straight away why you are writing.

Je me permets de vous écrire au sujet de votre annonce.I am writing to you regarding your ad.
Suite à notre échange téléphonique de ce matin, je vous envoie le devis.Following our phone conversation this morning, I'm sending you the quote.
Je vous écris pour vous demander un rendez-vous.I'm writing to ask you for an appointment.

Je me permets de… literally means “I take the liberty of…”. In English that sounds stiff, but in French it is a very common, polite way to start: learn je me permets de vous écrire as a fixed expression. Use vous by default in a first email; among colleagues, tu depends on the company.

", "

The body: attaching, asking, following up

Most professional emails do one of three things: send a document, ask for something, or follow up when nobody answers.

to…FrenchEnglish
attachVous trouverez ci-joint mon CV.Please find attached my résumé.
attachJe vous envoie ci-joint la facture.I'm attaching the invoice.
askPourriez-vous me confirmer la date ?Could you confirm the date?
askJe souhaiterais savoir si le prix comprend la livraison.I would like to know whether the price includes delivery.
askSerait-il possible de décaler le rendez-vous ?Would it be possible to move the meeting?
follow upJe me permets de revenir vers vous concernant ma commande.I'm following up regarding my order.
follow upSauf erreur de ma part, nous n'avons pas reçu votre paiement.Unless I'm mistaken, we haven't received your payment.
apologizeJe vous prie de m'excuser pour ce retard.Please accept my apologies for the delay.

Requests use the conditional you learned in the A2 level: pourriez-vous, je souhaiterais, serait-il possible. A plain present (Pouvez-vous… ?) is fine too, but the conditional is softer. Never use the imperative with a client: “Send me the file” is too direct.

Ci-joint (attached) is fixed before the noun: ci-joint la facture, ci-joint les documents. Revenir vers quelqu'un is office jargon for “to get back to someone”: Je reviens vers vous demain.

Un devis is a quote (an estimate of price), une facture an invoice, une commande an order. And the subject line of an email is l'objet: Objet : demande de devis.

", "

Closing the email

The ending comes in two parts: a last polite sentence, then the sign-off.

FrenchEnglish
Je reste à votre disposition pour tout renseignement complémentaire.Please don't hesitate to contact me if you need any further information.
Dans l'attente de votre réponse,I look forward to your reply,
Je vous remercie par avance.Thank you in advance.
Cordialement, / Bien cordialement,Best regards, / Kind regards,
Bonne journée, / Belle journée,Have a nice day,

Cordialement is the all-purpose sign-off; it does not mean “cordially” in a warm sense, just “regards”. Among close colleagues you may see Bonne journée, À demain or even Bises, but never with a client.

The very formal letter

For an official letter (an administration, a resignation), you will read: Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées. or Veuillez agréer, Madame, l'expression de mes sentiments distingués. Just recognize these: they are the French equivalent of “Yours faithfully”.

A complete email

Objet : demande de devis
Madame, Monsieur,
Suite à notre échange téléphonique, je me permets de vous écrire au sujet de votre offre. Pourriez-vous m'envoyer un devis pour vingt chaises ? Vous trouverez ci-joint le plan de la salle.
Je vous remercie par avance et reste à votre disposition.
Bien cordialement,
Camille RobertSubject: request for a quote. Dear Sir or Madam, Following our phone conversation, I am writing regarding your offer. Could you send me a quote for twenty chairs? Please find attached the floor plan of the room. Thank you in advance; please let me know if you need anything else. Kind regards, Camille Robert

In French, after the greeting and its comma, the next line starts with a capital letter: Madame, Monsieur, then Je me permets…
